claim: Hdac1 RNA expression level is the highest among all HDACs examined from zygote to beginning of neurula stage in Xenopus tropicalis.
source: The RNA expression level of hdac1 is the highest among all HDACs examined, followed by hdac2 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by temporal RNA expression profiles from ribo-depleted RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: Hdac1 and Hdac2 proteins are present from unfertilized egg to mid gastrula stage.
source: Both Hdac1 and Hdac2 proteins are present in the unfertilized egg to the mid gastrula stage, and the overall expression levels of Hdac1 and Hdac2 are relatively constant during this period (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by western blot analyses shown in Figure 1A

claim: Hdac1 and Hdac2 are the major maternally endowed HDACs functioning during early Xenopus development.
source: These data reveal that Hdac1/2 are the major maternally endowed HDACs functioning during this window of development.
evidence: Based on RNA expression profiles and protein expression data showing Hdac1/2 are most abundant

claim: Hdac1 binds to 1340 regions at mid-blastula (st8).
source: Hdac1 binds to 1340 regions at the mid-blastula (st8), 5136 regions at the late blastula (st9), and 22,681 regions at the early gastrula (st10.5) stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: Determined by ChIP-seq with IDR analysis

claim: Hdac1 binds to 5136 regions at late blastula (st9).
source: Hdac1 binds to 1340 regions at the mid-blastula (st8), 5136 regions at the late blastula (st9), and 22,681 regions at the early gastrula (st10.5) stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: Determined by ChIP-seq with IDR analysis

claim: Hdac1 binds to 22,681 regions at early gastrula (st10.5).
source: Hdac1 binds to 1340 regions at the mid-blastula (st8), 5136 regions at the late blastula (st9), and 22,681 regions at the early gastrula (st10.5) stages (Figure 1B).
evidence: Determined by ChIP-seq with IDR analysis

claim: Hdac1 progressively binds to the zygotic genome from mid-blastula and onward.
source: Here, we show that histone deacetylase 1 (Hdac1) progressively binds to the zygotic genome from mid-blastula and onward.
evidence: Supported by ChIP-seq data showing increasing numbers of Hdac1 binding sites across developmental stages

claim: The majority of Hdac1 peaks are present across multiple stages and at early gastrula stage.
source: Overall, a minority of Hdac1 peaks are unique to each of the blastula stages (Clusters a and b) and a majority of Hdac1 peaks are present across multiple stages (Cluster c) and at the early gastrula stage (Cluster d) (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: Based on clustered heatmap analysis of Hdac1 ChIP-seq signals

claim: Genes associated with sustained Hdac1 binding (Cluster c) are more active during gastrulation than genes in other clusters.
source: The expression levels of zygotic genes associated with Cluster c Hdac1 peaks are higher than those associated with Clusters a, b, and d, suggesting that the genes associated with sustained Hdac1 binding are more active during gastrulation (Figure 1D).
evidence: Based on TPM expression analysis of genes associated with different Hdac1 clusters

claim: Hdac2 gradually accumulates on the embryonic genome.
source: Similarly, Hdac2 gradually accumulates on the embryonic genome (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by Hdac2 ChIP-seq data

claim: 99% of Hdac1 peaks at stage 9 overlap with Hdac2 peaks.
source: Interestingly, 99% of Hdac1 peaks at stage 9 and 97% of Hdac1 peaks at stage 10.5 overlap with Hdac2 peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Based on Venn diagram comparison of Hdac1 and Hdac2 ChIP-seq peaks

claim: 97% of Hdac1 peaks at stage 10.5 overlap with Hdac2 peaks.
source: Interestingly, 99% of Hdac1 peaks at stage 9 and 97% of Hdac1 peaks at stage 10.5 overlap with Hdac2 peaks (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Based on Venn diagram comparison of Hdac1 and Hdac2 ChIP-seq peaks

claim: Hdac1 peaks display significantly higher Hdac2 peak enrichment compared to Hdac2 peaks without Hdac1.
source: When the levels of Hdac2 peaks associated with Hdac1 were compared to Hdac2 peaks , Hdac1 peaks display a significantly higher Hdac2 peak enrichment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Based on violin plot analysis comparing Hdac2 signal intensity

claim: The majority of Hdac1 peaks are found in either intergenic or intronic regions.
source: The majority of Hdac1 peaks are found in either intergenic or intronic regions; a minor fraction of Hdac1 peaks is present within exons or transcriptional termination sites.
evidence: Based on genomic feature annotation of Hdac1 peaks shown in Figure 1E

claim: Hdac1 binding to promoter regions increases over developmental time.
source: A notable observation is the increased Hdac1 binding to more promoter regions over developmental times (Figure 1E).
evidence: Based on distribution analysis of Hdac1 peaks across genomic features at different stages

claim: Higher enrichment of Hdac1 binding is located near promoters of genes as development proceeds.
source: We then analyzed the distribution of Hdac1 across three stages along the gene bodies of genes bound by Hdac1. A higher enrichment of Hdac1 binding is located near the promoters of genes as development proceeds (Figure 1F).
evidence: Based on signal profile analysis along gene bodies

claim: The timing of Hdac1-binding accumulation coincides with the mid-blastula stage (st8).
source: Importantly, the timing of Hdac1-binding accumulation coincides with the mid-blastula stage (st8) (Figure 1G), suggesting that Hdac1 is involved in the epigenetic regulation of these genes during ZGA.
evidence: Based on ChIP-qPCR data showing Hdac1 enrichment at selected genomic regions

claim: Hdac1 is involved in the epigenetic regulation of genes during ZGA.
source: Importantly, the timing of Hdac1-binding accumulation coincides with the mid-blastula stage (st8) (Figure 1G), suggesting that Hdac1 is involved in the epigenetic regulation of these genes during ZGA.
evidence: Inferred from the timing of Hdac1 binding coinciding with ZGA

claim: Hdac1 binding is independent of zygotic transcription at late blastula stage.
source: We conclude that Hdac1 binding is independent of zygotic transcription at the late blastula stage, suggesting the importance of maternal factors in Hdac1 recruitment.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq analysis of Hdac1 in α-amanitin-injected embryos showing high correlation with uninjected embryos

claim: Maternal factors are important for Hdac1 recruitment at late blastula stage.
source: We conclude that Hdac1 binding is independent of zygotic transcription at the late blastula stage, suggesting the importance of maternal factors in Hdac1 recruitment.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that Hdac1 binding is independent of zygotic transcription

claim: Sox, Foxh1, and Pou motifs are the most frequent maternal TF motifs in Hdac1 peaks at stage 9.
source: We, therefore, speculate that maternal factors instruct early Hdac1 recruitment. Our results provide evidence that maternal Foxh1/Sox3 plays a role in Hdac1 genomic recruitment (Figure 2E, F), highlighting the importance of these two maternal TFs in early embryonic epigenome establishment.
evidence: Based on de novo motif search of DNA sequences of st9 Hdac1 peaks shown in Figure 2B

claim: More than 80% of Hdac1 peaks overlap with Foxh1 or Sox3 peaks.
source: More than 80% of Hdac1 peaks overlap with Foxh1 or Sox3 peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E).
evidence: Based on Venn diagram analysis of peak overlaps

claim: A positive correlation exists between Hdac1 binding and Foxh1/Sox3 binding at all Hdac1 IDR peaks.
source: A positive correlation between Hdac1 binding and Foxh1/Sox3 binding is observed at all Hdac1 IDR peaks (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F, G).
evidence: Based on scatter plot analysis showing correlation between binding signals

claim: Hdac1 co-occupies genomic regions with Foxh1 and Sox3 on the same DNA molecules.
source: We confirmed the co-occupancy of Hdac1 with each of Foxh1 and Sox3 TFs on the same DNA molecules using sequential ChIP-qPCR (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1K, L).
evidence: Confirmed by sequential ChIP-qPCR experiments

claim: Depletion of Foxh1, Sox3, or both reduces Hdac1 binding around Foxh1/Sox3 co-occupied genomic regions.
source: Depletion of Foxh1, Sox3, or both TFs by morpholino injections showed a reduced binding of Hdac1 around Foxh1/Sox3 co-occupied genomic regions (Figure 2F).
evidence: Based on ChIP-qPCR analysis after morpholino-mediated depletion

claim: Foxh1 and Sox3 maternal TFs facilitate Hdac1 recruitment during ZGA.
source: Hence, we propose that Foxh1 and Sox3 maternal TFs facilitate Hdac1 recruitment during ZGA.
evidence: Based on motif analysis, co-occupancy data, and depletion experiments

claim: Ep300 binding is observed in Hdac1 peaks from late blastula and onward.
source: Ep300 binding (a HAT), which catalyzes the acetylation of histone, is observed in Hdac1 peaks (Clusters b–d) from the late blastula and onward where RNA polymerase II signals also emerge (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data showing Ep300 signals at Hdac1 peaks

claim: Hdac1 and Ep300 share similar binding profiles on many transcriptionally active genes.
source: This indicates that Hdac1 and Ep300 share similar binding profiles on many transcriptionally active genes.
evidence: Inferred from overlapping binding patterns of Hdac1 and Ep300

claim: Hdac1 peaks display signals of H3K9ac, H3K18ac, H3K27ac, and pan-H3Kac.
source: Consistent with the overlapping binding of Ep300, Hdac1 peaks display signals of H3K9ac (Clusters c and d), H3K18ac (Clusters b–d), H3K27ac (Clusters b–d), and pan-H3 lysine acetylation (pan-H3Kac) (Clusters b–d).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data for various histone acetylation marks shown in Figure 3A

claim: H3K4me1 and H3K4me3 display signals at Hdac1-bound regions (Clusters c and d).
source: H3K4me1, a primed enhancer mark (Creyghton et al., 2010), and H3K4me3, an active promoter mark (Heintzman et al., 2007), display signals at Hdac1-bound regions (Clusters c and d); H3K36me3, a transcription elongation mark (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009), displays minimal signals at any Hdac1-bound regions.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data for histone methylation marks shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, with citations to prior literature

claim: H3K36me3 displays minimal signals at any Hdac1-bound regions.
source: H3K4me1, a primed enhancer mark (Creyghton et al., 2010), and H3K4me3, an active promoter mark (Heintzman et al., 2007), display signals at Hdac1-bound regions (Clusters c and d); H3K36me3, a transcription elongation mark (Kolasinska-Zwierz et al., 2009), displays minimal signals at any Hdac1-bound regions.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data for histone methylation marks shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B, with citations to prior literature

claim: Hdac1 binds to genomic regions with active epigenetic signatures.
source: These observations reveal that Hdac1 binds to genomic regions with active epigenetic signatures.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of active histone marks at Hdac1-bound regions

claim: Hdac1 binds to genomic regions mostly free of H3K9me2, H3K9me3, or H4K20me3.
source: Hdac1 binds to genomic regions mostly free of H3K9me2, H3K9me3, or H4K20me3.
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data for repressive histone methylation marks shown in Figure 3B

claim: H3K9me2, H3K9me3, and H4K20me3 mark constitutive heterochromatin denoting gene-poor areas consisting of tandem repeats.
source: All three modifications are known to mark constitutive heterochromatin denoting gene-poor areas consisting of tandem repeats (Richards and Elgin, 2002).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge cited from Richards and Elgin, 2002

claim: A fraction of Hdac1-bound regions (Clusters c and d) display signals of H3K27me3.
source: In addition, a fraction of Hdac1-bound regions (Clusters c and d) display signals of H3K27me3 (Figure 3B), which is known to mark facultative heterochromatin consisting of developmental-cue silenced genes (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 3B, with citation to prior literature

claim: H3K27me3 marks facultative heterochromatin consisting of developmental-cue silenced genes.
source: In addition, a fraction of Hdac1-bound regions (Clusters c and d) display signals of H3K27me3 (Figure 3B), which is known to mark facultative heterochromatin consisting of developmental-cue silenced genes (Trojer and Reinberg, 2007).
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge cited from Trojer and Reinberg, 2007

claim: Hdac1 binds to facultative heterochromatic regions facilitating the repression of genes.
source: These observations suggest that Hdac1 binds to facultative heterochromatic regions facilitating the repression of genes.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of H3K27me3 at Hdac1-bound regions

claim: Hdac1 Cluster I peaks (3548 peaks) are marked by both H3K27ac and H3K27me3, representing heterogeneous CRMs.
source: Cluster I denotes 3548 Hdac1 peaks marked by both H3K27ac and H3K27me3 (Figure 3D). Given that both H3K27ac and H3K27me3 are modified on the same lysine residue, we speculate that these regions are differentially marked in space due to heterogeneous cell populations present in the whole embryo. Therefore, Hdac1 Cluster I peaks are referred to as heterogeneous CRMs.
evidence: Based on peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: Hdac1 Cluster II peaks (1389 peaks) are marked by only H3K27me3, representing repressive CRMs.
source: Cluster II denotes 1389 Hdac1 peaks marked by only H3K27me3 indicating that these regions are associated with inactive developmental genes (Figure 3D). Hdac1 Cluster II peaks represent repressive CRMs.
evidence: Based on peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: Hdac1 Cluster III peaks (13,669 peaks) are marked by only H3K27ac, representing active CRMs.
source: Cluster III denotes 13,669 Hdac1 peaks marked by only H3K27ac, suggesting that these are active CRMs.
evidence: Based on peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: Hdac1 Cluster IV peaks (4836 peaks) have neither H3K27ac nor H3K27me3 modifications.
source: Cluster IV denotes 4836 Hdac1 peaks with neither H3K27ac nor H3K27me3 modifications (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on peak overlap analysis shown in Figure 3C and 3D

claim: Expression levels of genes bound by Hdac1 are generally higher than genes unbound by Hdac1 at genomic loci marked with two distinct H3K27 modifications.
source: At genomic loci marked with two distinct H3K27 modifications (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), the expression levels of genes bound by Hdac1 (I, II, and III) are generally higher than that of genes unbound (I', II', and III') (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that Hdac1 binding correlates with transcriptional activity of the genes.
evidence: Based on expression analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1E

claim: Hdac1 binding correlates with transcriptional activity of genes.
source: At genomic loci marked with two distinct H3K27 modifications (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D), the expression levels of genes bound by Hdac1 (I, II, and III) are generally higher than that of genes unbound (I', II', and III') (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E), suggesting that Hdac1 binding correlates with transcriptional activity of the genes.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of expression levels between Hdac1-bound and unbound genes

claim: Embryos treated with TSA are developmentally arrested at gastrula.
source: Embryos treated with TSA are developmentally arrested at gastrula (Figure 4A).
evidence: Based on phenotypic observation of TSA-treated embryos shown in Figure 4A

claim: The dorsal blastopore lip is present in TSA-treated embryos, suggesting that the progression but not the initiation of gastrulation is defective.
source: We observed the presence of dorsal blastopore lip, suggesting that the progression but not the initiation of gastrulation is defective.
evidence: Based on morphological observation of TSA-treated embryos

claim: Valproic acid (VPA) produces a similar phenotype to TSA treatment.
source: A Class I HDAC inhibitor, valproic acid (VPA) (Göttlicher et al., 2001), also produces a similar phenotype (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on phenotypic observation shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, with citation to prior literature

claim: Protein levels of Hdac1 and Hdac2 are not affected by TSA treatment.
source: We first showed that protein levels of Hdac1 and Hdac2 are not affected by TSA treatment (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: TSA treatment does not alter the recruitment of Hdac1 to the genome.
source: These results suggest that TSA treatment of early Xenopus embryos does not alter the recruitment of Hdac1 to the genome.
evidence: Based on high Pearson correlations and minimal differential peaks between TSA-treated and control embryos

claim: Drastically increased levels of H3K9ac, H3K18ac, and H3K27ac are observed in TSA-treated embryos.
source: Drastically increased levels of H3K9ac, H3K18ac, and H3K27ac are observed in TSA-treated embryos (Figure 4B; Rao and LaBonne, 2018), whereas H3K14ac, H3K56ac, and H4K20ac are not detected during this stage of development.
evidence: Based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 4B, with citation to prior work

claim: H3K14ac, H3K56ac, and H4K20ac are not detected during gastrulation stage.
source: Drastically increased levels of H3K9ac, H3K18ac, and H3K27ac are observed in TSA-treated embryos (Figure 4B; Rao and LaBonne, 2018), whereas H3K14ac, H3K56ac, and H4K20ac are not detected during this stage of development.
evidence: Based on western blot analysis shown in Figure 4B

claim: HDAC activity is required to maintain the proper level of histone acetylation during gastrulation.
source: These data indicate that HDAC activity is required to maintain the proper level of histone acetylation during gastrulation.
evidence: Inferred from increased histone acetylation upon HDAC inhibition

claim: A majority (~75%) of pan-H3Kac are specifically marked in ectodermal (~37%) and endodermal (~38%) germ layers.
source: A comparison of high-confidence peaks from each explant reveals that a majority (~75%) of pan-H3Kac are specifically marked in ectodermal (~37%) and endodermal (~38%) germ layers (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on pan-H3Kac ChIP-seq analysis in dissected AC and VG explants

claim: The signal intensity of pan-H3Kac in AC/VG shared genomic regions is significantly higher than those of AC- or VG-specific genomic regions.
source: We observed the signal intensity of pan-H3Kac in AC/VG shared genomic regions (Cluster A in Figure 4C) is significantly higher than those of AC- or VG-specific genomic regions (Clusters B and C in Figure 4C), which also coincides with higher gene expression levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: Based on pan-H3Kac ChIP-seq signal analysis shown in Figure 4C and expression analysis in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C

claim: Expression levels of genes enriched with AC-specific pan-H3Kac are higher in AC than VG.
source: Indeed, the expression level of genes enriched with AC-specific pan-H3Kac are higher in AC than VG (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), and the expression levels of genes enriched with VG-specific pan-H3Kac are higher in VG than AC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis of dissected tissues shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: Expression levels of genes enriched with VG-specific pan-H3Kac are higher in VG than AC.
source: Indeed, the expression level of genes enriched with AC-specific pan-H3Kac are higher in AC than VG (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D), and the expression levels of genes enriched with VG-specific pan-H3Kac are higher in VG than AC (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq analysis of dissected tissues shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E

claim: The histone acetylation profile generally coincides with the animally and vegetally localized expression of transcripts.
source: These results illustrate that the histone acetylation profile generally coincides with the animally and vegetally localized expression of transcripts.
evidence: Based on correlation between pan-H3Kac patterns and gene expression in different germ layers

claim: A global increase of pan-H3Kac signals across all Hdac1 CRM Clusters is observed after TSA treatment.
source: A global increase of pan-H3Kac signals across all Hdac1 CRM Clusters is observed after TSA treatment (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), which is consistent with the western blot data (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on quantitative ChIP-seq analysis shown in Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 3A

claim: TSA-induced HDAC inhibition leads to elevated pan-H3Kac signals on both readily acetylated genomic loci and other genomic regions.
source: TSA-induced HDAC inhibition leads to elevated pan-H3Kac signals on both readily acetylated genomic loci (Cluster α of Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C) and other genomic regions (Cluster β of Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C).
evidence: Based on clustered heatmap analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3B, C

claim: Repressive CRMs (Cluster II, only H3K27me3) show the highest fold increase of pan-H3Kac signals upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Interestingly, we found that CRMs of Hdac1 Clusters I–IV respond differently upon HDAC inhibition: repressive CRMs (Cluster II, only H3K27me3) show the highest fold increase of pan-H3Kac signals, while active CRMs (Cluster III, only H3K27ac) show the lowest fold increase of pan-H3Kac signals when compared to other clusters (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Based on fold change analysis shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3D

claim: Active CRMs (Cluster III, only H3K27ac) show the lowest fold increase of pan-H3Kac signals upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Interestingly, we found that CRMs of Hdac1 Clusters I–IV respond differently upon HDAC inhibition: repressive CRMs (Cluster II, only H3K27me3) show the highest fold increase of pan-H3Kac signals, while active CRMs (Cluster III, only H3K27ac) show the lowest fold increase of pan-H3Kac signals when compared to other clusters (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Based on fold change analysis shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 3D

claim: The increased amount of pan-H3Kac is very similar across different Hdac1 clusters, irrespective of CRMs being repressive or active.
source: We also note that the increased amount of pan-H3Kac is very similar across different Hdac1 clusters, irrespective of CRMs being repressive or active CRMs (Figure 4—figure supplement 3E, F).
evidence: Based on signal analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3E, F

claim: HDACs catalytic activities are similar whether CRMs are repressive or active.
source: This suggests that HDACs catalytic activities are similar whether CRMs are repressive or active.
evidence: Inferred from similar amounts of pan-H3Kac increase across different CRM types

claim: Upon HDAC inhibition, Hdac1-bound repressive CRMs are subject to histone hyperacetylation.
source: In sum, upon HDAC inhibition, Hdac1-bound repressive CRMs are subject to histone hyperacetylation, while Hdac1-bound active CRMs exhibit a further increase of histone acetylation.
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of pan-H3Kac changes upon TSA treatment

claim: Upon HDAC inhibition, Hdac1-bound active CRMs exhibit a further increase of histone acetylation.
source: In sum, upon HDAC inhibition, Hdac1-bound repressive CRMs are subject to histone hyperacetylation, while Hdac1-bound active CRMs exhibit a further increase of histone acetylation.
evidence: Based on quantitative analysis of pan-H3Kac changes upon TSA treatment

claim: CRMs with low levels of histone acetylation tend to be more responsive to HDAC inhibition than CRMs with high levels of histone acetylation.
source: Interestingly, CRMs with low levels of histone acetylation tend to be more responsive to HDAC inhibition, than CRMs with high levels of histone acetylation.
evidence: Based on scatter plot analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3G

claim: Germ-layer-specific AC and VG CRMs show greater changes upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Germ-layer-specific AC and VG CRMs show the greater changes upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 4G).
evidence: Based on fold change analysis of spatial CRM categories shown in Figure 4G

claim: AC CRMs show an increase in pan-H3Kac signals in VG but not in AC after HDAC inhibition.
source: AC CRMs show an increase in pan-H3Kac signals in VG but not in AC after HDAC inhibition.
evidence: Based on fold change analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: VG CRMs acquire an increase of pan-H3Kac signals in AC but not in VG upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Similarly, VG CRMs acquire an increase of pan-H3Kac signals in AC but not in VG upon HDAC inhibition.
evidence: Based on fold change analysis shown in Figure 4G

claim: Hdac1 activity is spatially regulated in development to maintain proper germ layer specific gene expression patterns.
source: Taken together, these data demonstrate that Hdac1 activity is spatially regulated in development to maintain proper germ layer specific gene expression patterns.
evidence: Inferred from differential responses of germ-layer-specific CRMs to HDAC inhibition

claim: Class 1 genes (3104 genes) have CRMs with mixed marks of H3K27ac and/or H3K27me3, suggesting differential expression in different germ layers.
source: Class 1 denotes 3104 genes that have CRMs with mixed marks of H3K27ac and/or H3K27me3 suggesting that these genes are differentially expressed in different germ layers.
evidence: Based on gene classification according to CRM epigenetic marks shown in Figure 5A

claim: Class 2 genes (629 genes) have CRMs marked with only H3K27me3, indicating these genes may be repressed.
source: Class 2 denotes 629 genes whose CRMs are marked with only H3K27me3 indicating that these genes may be repressed.
evidence: Based on gene classification according to CRM epigenetic marks shown in Figure 5A

claim: Class 3 genes (5913 genes) have CRMs marked with only H3K27ac, suggesting these genes are differentially active in various germ layers.
source: Class 3 denotes 5913 genes whose CRMs are marked with only H3K27ac suggesting that these genes are differentially active in various germ layers.
evidence: Based on gene classification according to CRM epigenetic marks shown in Figure 5A

claim: Class 1 and 3 genes are continuously active after ZGA.
source: Class 1 and 3 genes are continuously active after ZGA, whereas Class 2 genes are gradually activated from early neurula and onward (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on extended temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Class 2 genes are gradually activated from early neurula and onward.
source: Class 1 and 3 genes are continuously active after ZGA, whereas Class 2 genes are gradually activated from early neurula and onward (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on extended temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Hdac1 regulates both transcriptionally active and silent genes at gastrulation.
source: These data suggest that Hdac1 regulates both transcriptionally active and silent genes at gastrulation.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of Hdac1 binding at genes with different expression states

claim: Greater than 85% of Class 2 genes are prematurely activated during gastrulation upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Interestingly, greater than 85% of Class 2 genes are prematurely activated during gastrulation upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5D), supporting the idea that Hdac1 temporally regulates the expression of Class 2 genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H ).
evidence: Based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: Hdac1 temporally regulates the expression of Class 2 genes.
source: Interestingly, greater than 85% of Class 2 genes are prematurely activated during gastrulation upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5D), supporting the idea that Hdac1 temporally regulates the expression of Class 2 genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H ).
evidence: Inferred from premature activation of Class 2 genes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Genes in Class 1 and 3 can be up- or down-regulated upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Furthermore, we observed that differentially regulated genes in Class 1 (CRMs are marked by a mixture of active H3K27ac and repressive H3K27me3) and Class 3 (whose CRMs are only marked by active H3K27ac) can be up- or down-regulated upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5D).
evidence: Based on differential expression analysis shown in Figure 5D

claim: HDAC activity on Class 1 and 3 genes is spatially regulated.
source: We speculate that HDAC activity Class 1 and 3 genes are spatially regulated.
evidence: Speculated based on observation of both up- and down-regulation of these genes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Genes normally expressed in the vegetal region (endoderm) are significantly up-regulated in AC upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Expression profiles of Class 1 genes revealed that genes normally expressed in the vegetal region (endoderm) are significantly up-regulated in AC upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5F, second bar).
evidence: Based on spatial expression analysis of differentially regulated genes shown in Figure 5F

claim: VG CRMs are hyperacetylated in AC upon HDAC inhibition, which leads to misactivation of endodermal genes in AC.
source: Coincidently, VG CRMs are hyperacetylated in AC upon HDAC inhibition (VG CRMs in Figure 4G), which in turn leads to the misactivation of endodermal genes in AC (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Based on correlation between histone acetylation changes and gene expression changes

claim: Genes normally expressed in ectoderm and mesoderm are significantly down-regulated in AC upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Surprisingly, we found that genes normally expressed in ectoderm and mesoderm are significantly down-regulated in AC upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5F, third bar) and genes normally expressed in mesoderm and endoderm are significantly down-regulated in VG (Figure 5F, fifth bar), upon HDAC inhibition.
evidence: Based on spatial expression analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: Genes normally expressed in mesoderm and endoderm are significantly down-regulated in VG upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Surprisingly, we found that genes normally expressed in ectoderm and mesoderm are significantly down-regulated in AC upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5F, third bar) and genes normally expressed in mesoderm and endoderm are significantly down-regulated in VG (Figure 5F, fifth bar), upon HDAC inhibition.
evidence: Based on spatial expression analysis shown in Figure 5F

claim: Hdac1 positively influences the transcription of active genes in each germ layer.
source: Contrary to the repressive role of Hdac1, this finding suggests that Hdac1 positively influences the transcription of active genes in each germ layer.
evidence: Inferred from down-regulation of germ-layer-specific genes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: The state of histone acetylation on CRMs associated with active genes is dynamic, and disruption to such equilibrium impairs normal transcription activities.
source: We propose that the state of histone acetylation on CRMs associated with active genes is dynamic, and disruption to such equilibrium impairs normal transcription activities.
evidence: Proposed based on observation that HDAC inhibition leads to reduced expression of active genes

claim: TSA-induced excessive histone acetylation on active CRMs may contribute to the attenuated expression of associated active genes in respective germ layers.
source: This TSA-induced excessive histone acetylation on active CRMs may contribute to the attenuated expression of associated active genes in respective germ layers (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Speculated based on correlation between excessive acetylation and reduced gene expression

claim: Hdac1 not only prevents aberrant activation of silent genes, but also maintains proper gene expression levels in each germ layer.
source: These data demonstrate that Hdac1 not only prevents aberrant activation of silent genes, but also maintains proper gene expression levels in each germ layer (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I,J).
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of gene expression changes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Class 1 genes display a higher variability in expression levels between different germ layers when compared to Class 3 genes.
source: Class 1 genes display a higher variability in expression levels between different germ layers when compared to Class 3 genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Based on standard deviation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1G

claim: The expression of genes undergoing active H3K27me3 suppression is more intimately associated with germ-layer determination.
source: This indicates that the expression of genes undergoing active H3K27me3 suppression is more intimately associated with germ-layer determination.
evidence: Inferred from higher expression variability of Class 1 genes between germ layers

claim: Hdac1 maintains the integrity of germ-layer genes both in time and space during gastrulation.
source: Altogether, these results show that Hdac1 maintains the integrity of germ-layer genes both in time and space during gastrulation.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of temporal and spatial gene expression changes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Progressive binding of Hdac1 to the genome shapes the zygotic histone acetylome, thereby reinforcing a proper germ-layer-specific transcriptome, both in time and space.
source: Our findings demonstrate a close link between homeostasis of histone acetylation and transcriptional activities in developing embryos. Progressive binding of Hdac1 to the genome shapes the zygotic histone acetylome, thereby reinforcing a proper germ-layer-specific transcriptome, both in time and space.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of Hdac1 binding, histone acetylation, and gene expression

claim: Hdac1 is an essential epigenetic regulator in the control of embryonic cell identity and lineage.
source: Thus, Hdac1 is an essential epigenetic regulator in the control of embryonic cell identity and lineage.
evidence: Concluded from the comprehensive role of Hdac1 in regulating histone acetylation and gene expression during development

claim: TFs inducing differentiation programs exploit the activity of HDACs to confine the expression of zygotic genes.
source: We propose that TFs inducing differentiation programs exploit the activity of HDACs to confine the expression of zygotic genes.
evidence: Proposed based on the role of maternal TFs in Hdac1 recruitment and Hdac1's role in gene regulation

claim: Zygotic transcription is dispensable for Hdac1 recruitment to the genome at late blastula.
source: Surprisingly, ChIP-seq analyses of Hdac1 from α-amanitin-injected embryos show that zygotic transcription is dispensable for Hdac1 recruitment to the genome, at the very least, up to late blastula (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq analysis in α-amanitin-injected embryos

claim: Active transcription is required to shape histone acetylation patterns in yeast largely due to a direct role of RNAPII in recruitment and activation of H4 HATs but not HDACs.
source: Recent work in yeast shows that active transcription is required to shape histone acetylation patterns largely due to a direct role of RNAPII in recruitment and activation of H4 HATs but not HDACs (Martin et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on cited work from Martin et al., 2021

claim: Hdac1 recruitment is not directed by on-going transcription.
source: Our result agrees with the notion that Hdac1 recruitment is not directed by on-going transcription.
evidence: Based on comparison with yeast studies and α-amanitin experiments

claim: Maternal Foxh1/Sox3 plays a role in Hdac1 genomic recruitment.
source: Our results provide evidence that maternal Foxh1/Sox3 plays a role in Hdac1 genomic recruitment (Figure 2E, F), highlighting the importance of these two maternal TFs in early embryonic epigenome establishment.
evidence: Based on motif analysis, co-occupancy, and depletion experiments

claim: Maternal TFs such as Foxh1, Vegt, and Otx1 bind the genome as early as the 32- to 64-cell stage.
source: Though maternal TFs such as Foxh1, Vegt, and Otx1 are shown to bind the genome as early as the 32- to 64-cell stage (Charney et al., 2017; Paraiso et al., 2019), the genome-wide binding of Hdac1 likely begins at blastula and is not significantly widespread until early gastrula (Figure 1C, G).
evidence: Based on cited work from Charney et al., 2017 and Paraiso et al., 2019

claim: The genome-wide binding of Hdac1 likely begins at blastula and is not significantly widespread until early gastrula.
source: Though maternal TFs such as Foxh1, Vegt, and Otx1 are shown to bind the genome as early as the 32- to 64-cell stage (Charney et al., 2017; Paraiso et al., 2019), the genome-wide binding of Hdac1 likely begins at blastula and is not significantly widespread until early gastrula (Figure 1C, G).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data showing progressive Hdac1 binding

claim: Hdac1 containing complexes bind to pre-existing epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and H3K4me3.
source: It is also known that Hdac1 containing complexes bind to pre-existing epigenetic marks such as DNA methylation and H3K4me3 (Wade et al., 1999; Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: Based on cited work from Wade et al., 1999 and Lee et al., 2018

claim: Maternally instructed histone modifications may play a role in Hdac1 recruitment.
source: Therefore, maternally instructed histone modifications may also play a role in Hdac1 recruitment.
evidence: Speculated based on known mechanisms of Hdac1 complex recruitment

claim: Hdac1 binds to repressive genomic regions that are facultative but not constitutive heterochromatin.
source: Hdac1 binds to repressive genomic regions that are facultative but not constitutive heterochromatin.
evidence: Based on analysis of histone methylation marks at Hdac1-bound regions

claim: The profile of H3K27me3 is largely different (~90% non-overlapping peaks) from profiles of H3K9me2, 3, and H4K20me3 in early Xenopus development.
source: Though histone modifications underlying constitutive heterochromatin have been shown to regulate developmental genes (Riddle et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2018; Methot et al., 2021), the profile of H3K27me3 is largely different (~90% non-overlapping peaks) from profiles of H3K9me2, 3, and H4K20me3 in early Xenopus development (data not shown, van Kruijsbergen et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on comparison of ChIP-seq data, with citations to prior literature

claim: Hdac1-mediated suppression is largely dictated by developmental programs.
source: These observations suggest that Hdac1-mediated suppression is largely dictated by developmental programs.
evidence: Inferred from the association of Hdac1 with facultative rather than constitutive heterochromatin

claim: The binding of Hdac1 at active genomic regions is consistent with previous studies in yeast and mammalian cell culture emphasizing a dynamic equilibrium of histone acetylation at active loci.
source: However, our findings are consistent with previous studies in yeast and mammalian cell culture emphasizing a dynamic equilibrium of histone acetylation at active loci (Kurdistani et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2009; Kidder and Palmer, 2012).
evidence: Based on comparison with cited prior studies

claim: Hdac1 functions at both active and inactive CRMs in early embryos.
source: Hence, we hypothesize that Hdac1 functions at both active and inactive CRMs in early embryos.
evidence: Hypothesized based on observation of Hdac1 binding at both active and repressive genomic regions

claim: An increase of pan-H3Kac is observed across Hdac1-bound CRMs, including active CRMs, consistent with the canonical enzymatic activity of Hdac1.
source: First, an increase of pan-H3Kac (detecting acetylated forms of H3K9, K14, K18, and K27) is observed across Hdac1-bound CRMs, including active CRMs, consistent with the canonical enzymatic activity of Hdac1 (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on quantitative ChIP-seq analysis upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Repressive CRMs marked by H3K27me3 undergo drastic H3 hyperacetylation compared to active CRMs marked by H3K27ac, suggesting HDAC-activity-dependent suppression of repressive CRMs.
source: Second, repressive CRMs marked by H3K27me3 undergo drastic H3 hyperacetylation compared to active CRMs marked by H3K27ac suggesting a HDAC-activity-dependent suppression of repressive CRMs (Figure 4F, Figure 4—figure supplement 3D).
evidence: Based on fold change analysis of pan-H3Kac upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Germ-layer-specific pan-H3Kac profiles are disrupted upon HDAC inhibition, indicating the importance of Hdac1 in defining spatial patterns of histone acetylation.
source: Third, germ-layer-specific pan-H3Kac profiles are disrupted indicating the importance of Hdac1 in defining spatial patterns of histone acetylation (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3I).
evidence: Based on analysis of spatial pan-H3Kac changes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: On inactive CRMs, Hdac1 prevents histone acetylation, thereby preserving H3K27 as unacetylated.
source: On the one hand, Hdac1 prevents histone acetylation at inactive CRMs, thereby preserving H3K27 as unacetylated (Figure 5G).
evidence: Based on model proposed from experimental data

claim: H3K27me3 is not always imposed on inactive CRMs.
source: Interestingly, H3K27me3 is not always imposed on inactive CRMs.
evidence: Based on observation that some inactive CRMs lack H3K27me3

claim: HDAC-mediated histone deacetylation and Polycomb-mediated histone methylation are not coupled at inactive CRMs.
source: This suggests that HDAC-mediated histone deacetylation and Polycomb-mediated histone methylation are not coupled at inactive CRMs.
evidence: Inferred from observation that H3K27me3 is not always present at inactive CRMs

claim: On active CRMs, Hdac1 participates in dynamic histone acetylation–deacetylation cycles.
source: On the other hand, Hdac1 participates in dynamic histone acetylation–deacetylation cycles at active CRMs (Figure 5H).
evidence: Based on model proposed from experimental data

claim: The binding profiles of Ep300 and Hdac1 mostly overlap.
source: Although we did not directly test the co-binding of HATs and HDACs, CRMs may be simultaneously bound since (1) the binding profiles of Ep300 and Hdac1 mostly overlap (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and (2) pan-H3Kac signals increase at all Hdac1 peaks including active CRMs, upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on ChIP-seq data comparison

claim: Pan-H3Kac signals increase at all Hdac1 peaks including active CRMs upon HDAC inhibition.
source: Although we did not directly test the co-binding of HATs and HDACs, CRMs may be simultaneously bound since (1) the binding profiles of Ep300 and Hdac1 mostly overlap (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A), and (2) pan-H3Kac signals increase at all Hdac1 peaks including active CRMs, upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Based on quantitative ChIP-seq analysis

claim: Active CRMs are maintained in a state of dynamic equilibrium.
source: Presumably, active CRMs are maintained in a state of dynamic equilibrium.
evidence: Speculated based on overlapping HAT/HDAC binding and response to HDAC inhibition

claim: HATs and HDACs simultaneously participate in histone acetylation cycles, which initiate and reset chromatin between rounds of transcription.
source: This model is in accordance with a previous study demonstrating that HATs and HDACs simultaneously participate in histone acetylation cycles, which initiate and reset chromatin between rounds of transcription (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited work from Wang et al., 2009

claim: Genes associated with repressive CRMs (H3K27me3 only) are mainly inactive until neurula.
source: Genes associated with repressive CRMs (H3K27me3 only) are mainly inactive until neurula (Figure 5C).
evidence: Based on temporal expression analysis shown in Figure 5C

claim: Hdac1 maintains the state of histone hypoacetylation on repressive CRMs, thereby preventing premature expression of genes.
source: More than 85% of these genes are prematurely activated upon HDAC inhibition (Figure 5D), suggesting that Hdac1 maintains the state of histone hypoacetylation on repressive CRMs, thereby preventing premature expression of genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: Inferred from premature activation of repressive CRM-associated genes upon HDAC inhibition

claim: Genes associated with heterogeneous and active CRMs are misactivated in different germ layers when HDAC activity is blocked.
source: Moreover, genes associated with heterogeneous (both H3K27ac and H3K27me3) and active (H3K27ac only) CRMs are misactivated in different germ layers when HDAC activity is blocked (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on spatial expression analysis of differentially regulated genes

claim: Hdac1 safeguards differential histone acetylation states in each germ layer, restricting proper spatial transcription.
source: This indicates that Hdac1 safeguards differential histone acetylation states in each germ layer (Figure 4G, Figure 4—figure supplement 3I), restricting proper spatial transcription (Figure 5—figure supplement 1I, J).
evidence: Inferred from misactivation of genes in inappropriate germ layers upon HDAC inhibition

claim: H3K27me3 is spatially deposited at late gastrula.
source: We did not directly address whether hypoacetylated heterogeneous CRMs are subjected to H3K27me3. However, a previous study showed that H3K27me3 is spatially deposited at late gastrula (Akkers et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited work from Akkers et al., 2009

claim: Heterogenous CRMs are differentially marked by opposing H3K27me3 or acetylation in different germ layers.
source: We predict that heterogenous CRMs are differentially marked by opposing H3K27me3 or acetylation in different germ layers.
evidence: Predicted based on spatial deposition of H3K27me3 and observed heterogeneous CRM patterns

claim: Hdac1 preserves the histone hypoacetylation state of inactive CRMs resulting in gene suppression both in time and space.
source: In summary, Hdac1 preserves the histone hypoacetylation state of inactive CRMs resulting in gene suppression both in time and space, thus supporting the transcriptional corepressor role for Hdac1.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of Hdac1 function at inactive CRMs

claim: Hdac1 plays a role in sustaining active gene expression during germ-layer formation.
source: Our study reveals an unexpected role for Hdac1 in sustaining active gene expression during germ-layer formation.
evidence: Based on observation that HDAC inhibition leads to down-regulation of active genes

claim: Within both ectoderm and endoderm, the expression of HDAC inhibitor down-regulated genes associated with either active or heterogeneous CRMs are enriched in their respective germ layers.
source: Within both ectoderm and endoderm, the expression of HDAC inhibitor down-regulated genes associated with either active (H3K27ac only) or heterogeneous (H3K27ac and H3K27me3) CRMs are enriched in their respective germ layers (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on spatial expression analysis of down-regulated genes

claim: A paradoxical activator role for Hdac1 has been reported in previous studies.
source: This suggests a paradoxical activator role for Hdac1, which is also reported in previous studies (Vidal and Gaber, 1991; Zupkovitz et al., 2006; Baltus et al., 2009; Hughes et al., 2014; Rao and LaBonne, 2018).
evidence: Based on cited prior studies

claim: Utilization of HDAC activities at active genomic loci is a general mechanism seen in Xenopus ectoderm and endoderm lineages.
source: We speculate that utilization of HDAC activities at active genomic loci is a general mechanism, as seen in examples of Xenopus ectoderm and endoderm lineages, which deploy distinct gene regulatory networks.
evidence: Speculated based on observation in two distinct germ layers

claim: A dynamic equilibrium between acetylation and deacetylation is essential to sustain gene transcription.
source: Based on our findings, we propose that a dynamic equilibrium between acetylation and deacetylation is essential to sustain gene transcription.
evidence: Proposed based on observation that HDAC inhibition reduces expression of active genes

claim: In yeast, cotranscriptional methylation (H3K36me3 and H3K4me2) recruits HDAC containing complexes (Rpd3S and Set3C) to suppress intragenic transcription and delay induction of genes that overlap non-coding RNAs.
source: In yeast, cotranscriptional methylation (H3K36me3 and H3K4me2) recruits HDAC containing complexes (Rpd3S and Set3C) to suppress intragenic transcription and delay induction of genes that overlap non-coding RNAs (Carrozza et al., 2005; Keogh et al., 2005; Li et al., 2007; Kim and Buratowski, 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Heo et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on cited prior studies in yeast

claim: Genetic deletion of Set3C affects transcript levels only in altered growth conditions.
source: Genetic deletion of Set3C affects transcript levels only in altered growth conditions (Lenstra et al., 2011), consistent with the notion that cyclical histone acetylation acts as a mechanism to regulate dynamics and fidelity of transcription.
evidence: Based on cited work from Lenstra et al., 2011

claim: HDAC1 can be targeted by Ep300 to transcribing genes through a direct interaction in metazoans.
source: In metazoans HDAC1 can be targeted by Ep300 to transcribing genes through a direct interaction (Simone et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on cited work from Simone et al., 2004

claim: Simultaneous binding of both HATs and HDACs at active genomic regions is shown in T cells.
source: Simultaneous binding of both HATs and HDACs at active genomic regions is shown in T cells (Wang et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited work from Wang et al., 2009

claim: Inhibition of both DNA methyltransferases and HDACs induces cryptic transcription in lung cancer cells.
source: Inhibition of both DNA methyltransferases and HDACs induces cryptic transcription in lung cancer cells (Brocks et al., 2017).
evidence: Based on cited work from Brocks et al., 2017

claim: Down-regulated genes upon HDAC inhibition exhibit high levels of cryptic transcripts during mouse cardiogenesis.
source: Down-regulated genes upon HDAC inhibition exhibit high levels of cryptic transcripts during mouse cardiogenesis (Milstone et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited work from Milstone et al., 2020

claim: HDAC activity plays a role in transcriptional fidelity.
source: These findings suggest a role for HDAC activity in transcriptional fidelity.
evidence: Inferred from cited studies showing effects of HDAC inhibition on cryptic transcription

claim: Active and heterogeneous CRMs are excessively acetylated following HDAC inhibition, which results in reduced expression of these CRM-associated genes within their respective germ layers.
source: We observed that active (H3K27ac only) and heterogeneous (both H3K27ac and H3K27me3) CRMs are excessively acetylated (Figure 4E, Figure 4—figure supplement 3A) following HDAC inhibition, which results in the reduced expression of these CRM-associated genes within their respective germ layers (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Based on correlation between excessive acetylation and reduced gene expression

claim: Excessive histone acetylation interferes with the activity of the transcriptional machinery.
source: This leads us to speculate that excessive histone acetylation interferes the activity of the transcriptional machinery.
evidence: Speculated based on observation that excessive acetylation reduces gene expression

claim: Excessive histone acetylation on chromatin induced by inhibition of HDAC1, 2, and 3 leads to increased aberrant contacts and reduced native contacts between super-enhancer loops.
source: A recent study shows that excessive histone acetylation on chromatin induced by inhibition of HDAC1, 2, and 3 leads to increased aberrant contacts and reduced native contacts between super-enhancer loops (Gryder et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on cited work from Gryder et al., 2019

claim: Excessive histone acetylation impairs active transcription by altering chromatin interactions.
source: This suggests that the excessive histone acetylation impairs active transcription by altering chromatin interactions.
evidence: Inferred from cited study on chromatin loop alterations

claim: H4 polyacetylation induced by HDAC inhibition is preferentially bound by BRD proteins (such as BRD4), thereby sequestering these factors away from active genes.
source: Alternatively, excessive histone acetylation can alter the binding of acetyl-histone readers. H4 polyacetylation induced by HDAC inhibition is shown to be preferentially bound by BRD proteins (such as BRD4), thereby sequestering these factors away from active genes (Slaughter et al., 2021).
evidence: Based on cited work from Slaughter et al., 2021

claim: HDACs safeguard the function of normal acetyl-histone readers.
source: Therefore, HDACs safeguard the function of normal acetyl-histone readers.
evidence: Inferred from the sequestration of BRD proteins by excessive acetylation

claim: The recruitment of Hdac1 to the genome at blastula is instructed maternally.
source: The recruitment of Hdac1 to the genome at blastula is instructed maternally.
evidence: Based on α-amanitin experiments and maternal TF analysis

claim: Hdac1 not only represses gene expression by sustaining a histone hypoacetylation state on inactive chromatin, but also maintains gene expression through participating in dynamic histone acetylation–deacetylation cycles on active chromatin.
source: We highlight a dual function model of Hdac1 where Hdac1 not only represses gene expression by sustaining a histone hypoacetylation state on inactive chromatin, but also maintains gene expression through participating in dynamic histone acetylation–deacetylation cycles on active chromatin.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of Hdac1 function at different CRM types

claim: Hdac1 maintains differential histone acetylation states of bound CRMs between different germ layers and reinforces the transcriptional program underlying cell lineage identities, both in time and space.
source: As a result, Hdac1 maintains differential histone acetylation states of bound CRMs between different germ layers and reinforces the transcriptional program underlying cell lineage identities, both in time and space.
evidence: Based on comprehensive analysis of spatial and temporal gene regulation by Hdac1

claim: Histone acetylation plays an essential role in modulating zygotic transcription and cell lineage specification of developing embryos.
source: Histone acetylation is a pivotal epigenetic modification that controls chromatin structure and regulates gene expression. It plays an essential role in modulating zygotic transcription and cell lineage specification of developing embryos.
evidence: Based on established knowledge and the study's findings

claim: Histone acetylation appears during the onset of both minor and major ZGA waves in many species.
source: Histone acetylation appears during the onset of both minor and major ZGA waves in many species.
evidence: Based on established knowledge from multiple species

claim: In Drosophila, histone acetylation occurs at mitotic cycle 8 on a few early zygotic genes.
source: In Drosophila, histone acetylation occurs at mitotic cycle 8 on a few early zygotic genes (Li et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited work from Li et al., 2014

claim: miR430, the first zygotically active gene, is marked by H3K27ac in 64-cell staged zebrafish embryos.
source: miR430, the first zygotically active gene, is marked by H3K27ac in 64-cell staged zebrafish embryos (Chan et al., 2019).
evidence: Based on cited work from Chan et al., 2019

claim: Genome-wide H3K27ac is detected at mid-blastula shortly after the onset of ZGA in Xenopus.
source: Genome-wide H3K27ac is detected at mid-blastula shortly after the onset of ZGA in Xenopus (Gupta et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on cited work from Gupta et al., 2014

claim: In mice, the zygotic genome is increasingly marked by H3K27ac from immature and metaphase II oocytes to 2-cell-stage embryos.
source: In mice, the zygotic genome is increasingly marked by H3K27ac from immature and metaphase II oocytes to 2-cell-stage embryos (Dahl et al., 2016).
evidence: Based on cited work from Dahl et al., 2016

claim: Histone acetylation occurs on the ε-amino group of the lysine residues within N-terminal tails of all four core histones.
source: Histone acetylation occurs on the ε-amino group of the lysine residues within N-terminal tails of all four core histones (Inoue and Fujimoto, 1969; Seto and Yoshida, 2014).
evidence: Based on cited work from Inoue and Fujimoto, 1969 and Seto and Yoshida, 2014

claim: Acetylation is a reversible process that is directly catalyzed by opposing activities of histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs).
source: Acetylation is a reversible process that is directly catalyzed by opposing activities of histone acetyltransferases (HATs) and histone deacetylases (HDACs).
evidence: Based on established knowledge

claim: HATs and HDACs can regulate the acetylation of lysine residues on non-histone proteins.
source: In addition, HATs and HDACs can also regulate the acetylation of lysine residues on non-histone proteins (Choudhary et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on cited work from Choudhary et al., 2009

claim: Histone acetylation is often associated with active gene transcription because the acyl groups neutralize the positive charge on the lysine residues, thereby reducing the affinity of histones to DNA.
source: Histone acetylation is often associated with active gene transcription because the acyl groups neutralize the positive charge on the lysine residues, thereby reducing the affinity of histones to DNA (Wang et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2001); it also serves as a binding platform for bromodomain (BRD) proteins which scaffold and stimulate the transcriptional machinery (Hassan et al., 2007; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on cited work from Wang et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2001; Hassan et al., 2007; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012

claim: Histone acetylation serves as a binding platform for bromodomain (BRD) proteins which scaffold and stimulate the transcriptional machinery.
source: Histone acetylation is often associated with active gene transcription because the acyl groups neutralize the positive charge on the lysine residues, thereby reducing the affinity of histones to DNA (Wang et al., 2000; Anderson et al., 2001); it also serves as a binding platform for bromodomain (BRD) proteins which scaffold and stimulate the transcriptional machinery (Hassan et al., 2007; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).
evidence: Based on cited work from Hassan et al., 2007 and Filippakopoulos et al., 2012

claim: The balance between HATs and HDACs directly shapes histone acetylation landscapes and subsequently affects transcriptomes.
source: The balance between HATs and HDACs directly shapes histone acetylation landscapes and subsequently affects transcriptomes.
evidence: Based on established knowledge and the study's findings

claim: HDACs are critical epigenetic regulators because they reset chromatin states by returning acetylated lysine residues on histones to the basal state, which can subsequently be subjected to alternative modifications such as methylation.
source: HDACs are critical epigenetic regulators because they reset chromatin states by returning acetylated lysine residues on histones to the basal state, which can subsequently be subjected to alternative modifications such as methylation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge

claim: HDACs are grouped into four classes based on phylogenetic conservation: Class I (HDAC1, 2, 3, 8), Class II (HDAC4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10), Class III (SIRT1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7), and Class IV (HDAC11).
source: HDACs are grouped into four classes based on phylogenetic conservation. Class I (HDAC1, 2, 3, 8), Class II (HDAC4, 5, 6, 7, 9, 10), and Class IV (HDAC11) HDACs are zinc dependent and are related to yeast Rpd3, Had1, and Hos3, respectively; Class III (SIRT1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7) HDACs, also known as Sirtuins, are NAD+ dependent and are related to yeast Sir2 (Gregoretti et al., 2004; Milazzo et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited work from Gregoretti et al., 2004 and Milazzo et al., 2020

claim: Hdac1 silences homeotic genes in cooperation with Polycomb group repressors in Drosophila.
source: For example, Hdac1 silences homeotic genes in cooperation with Polycomb group repressors in Drosophila (Chang et al., 2001).
evidence: Based on cited work from Chang et al., 2001

claim: In zebrafish, Hdac1 represses Notch targets during neurogenesis.
source: In zebrafish, Hdac1 represses Notch targets during neurogenesis (Cunliffe, 2004; Yamaguchi et al., 2005).
evidence: Based on cited work from Cunliffe, 2004 and Yamaguchi et al., 2005

claim: In Xenopus, HDAC activity suppresses Vegt-induced ectopic mesoderm in ectoderm lineages.
source: In Xenopus, HDAC activity suppresses Vegt-induced ectopic mesoderm in ectoderm lineages (Gao et al., 2016), represses multi-lineage marker genes at blastula (Rao and LaBonne, 2018), and desensitizes dorsal Wnt signaling at late blastula (Esmaeili et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited work from Gao et al., 2016

claim: In Xenopus, HDAC activity represses multi-lineage marker genes at blastula.
source: In Xenopus, HDAC activity suppresses Vegt-induced ectopic mesoderm in ectoderm lineages (Gao et al., 2016), represses multi-lineage marker genes at blastula (Rao and LaBonne, 2018), and desensitizes dorsal Wnt signaling at late blastula (Esmaeili et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited work from Rao and LaBonne, 2018

claim: In Xenopus, HDAC activity desensitizes dorsal Wnt signaling at late blastula.
source: In Xenopus, HDAC activity suppresses Vegt-induced ectopic mesoderm in ectoderm lineages (Gao et al., 2016), represses multi-lineage marker genes at blastula (Rao and LaBonne, 2018), and desensitizes dorsal Wnt signaling at late blastula (Esmaeili et al., 2020).
evidence: Based on cited work from Esmaeili et al., 2020

claim: Inhibition of HDAC activities rapidly down-regulates some genes in yeast, suggesting an activator function of HDACs.
source: For instance, inhibition of HDAC activities rapidly down-regulates some genes in yeast, suggesting an activator function of HDACs (Bernstein et al., 2000).
evidence: Based on cited work from Bernstein et al., 2000

claim: Genetic deletions or pharmacological application of HDAC inhibitors in cell lines results in both up- and down-regulation of genes.
source: Genetic deletions or pharmacological application of HDAC inhibitors in cell lines results in both up- and down-regulation of genes (Reid et al., 2005; Zupkovitz et al., 2006; Meganathan et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited work from Reid et al., 2005; Zupkovitz et al., 2006; Meganathan et al., 2015

claim: Genome-wide studies showed that HDACs occupy genomic loci of active genes, and their binding correlates with gene activities.
source: Furthermore, genome-wide studies showed that HDACs occupy genomic loci of active genes, and their binding correlates with gene activities (Kurdistani et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2009; Kidder and Palmer, 2012).
evidence: Based on cited work from Kurdistani et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2002; Wang et al., 2009; Kidder and Palmer, 2012

claim: Current evidence in Xenopus and other non-mammalian systems suggests that the early embryonic genome is rather naive and that major chromatin modifications occur at or after ZGA.
source: Current evidence in Xenopus as well as in other non-mammalian systems suggests that the early embryonic genome is rather naive and that major chromatin modifications occur at or after ZGA (Bonn et al., 2012; Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Gupta et al., 2014; van Heeringen et al., 2014; Hontelez et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on cited work from Bonn et al., 2012; Vastenhouw et al., 2010; Gupta et al., 2014; van Heeringen et al., 2014; Hontelez et al., 2015
